title: The Afternoon Brief: Judge Vacates Visa Ban as Water Cuts, Fire, Strike Add Up
dek: A federal judge's 61-page ruling striking down the administration's 75-country visa freeze anchored a day that also brought mandatory Colorado River cuts, a Nevada wildfire emergency, and new detail on a fatal federal shooting in Memphis.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: A federal judge found the administration's 75-country visa freeze unlawful and ordered denials made solely under it reconsidered, while separate developments on water, fire, tariffs, and a Memphis shooting each opened new questions rather than closing them.
bottom_line: A federal judge vacated the administration's 75-country visa freeze as unlawful, ordering reconsideration of denials made solely under it, while the Interior Department locked in two years of mandatory Colorado River cuts for California, Nevada and Arizona without resolving the longer-term allocation question. Separately, a Nevada wildfire emergency, a fatal drone strike in Kryvyi Rih, new detail on a federal shooting in Memphis, and tariffs now in effect between the U.S. and Canada each mark stages in ongoing situations rather than conclusions. The sourcing is detailed on the legal reasoning behind the visa ruling and the terms of the water and TikTok settlements, but silent on whether the administration will appeal and on what caused U.S.-Canada talks to collapse. Coming checkpoints include a possible State Department appeal, the September 8 Canadian retaliatory tariffs, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation's findings on the Neal shooting, and whether reservoir levels prompt deeper river cuts before 2029.
body: The day's throughline is a series of processes moving to new stages without resolving: a court ruling that vacates a policy but leaves an appeal question open, a river-management mandate that solves two years but not ten, a fire burning in real time, and an investigation into a shooting that has not yet reached a charging decision.

The central story is U.S. District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas's 61-page opinion striking down the State Department's policy suspending immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries. Announced in January, the policy had directed embassies and consulates to halt immigrant visa adjudications for citizens of countries including Afghanistan, Brazil and Yemen, with the State Department saying it aimed to "prevent the entry of foreign nationals who would take welfare and public benefits." Judge Vargas found the policy violated the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952's bar on nationality-based discrimination in visa issuance and exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio's statutory authority, writing "In many ways, this is not a challenging case." The ruling vacates the ban and requires consular officers to reconsider, under normal immigration law, any visa denials made solely under the policy. Plaintiffs' attorneys, including Susan Welber of The Legal Aid Society and Antionette Dozier of the Western Center on Law & Poverty, said the policy was "premised on a fiction" and that the ruling means "a return to fair, case-by-case review." A State Department spokesperson said the administration is "protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting" and does not comment on ongoing litigation.

The Interior Department separately mandated 1.25 million acre-feet in annual Colorado River water cuts for California, Nevada and Arizona for 2027 and 2028, with Arizona absorbing the largest share at 760,000 acre-feet, California 440,000 acre-feet, and Nevada 50,000 acre-feet, based on a voluntary agreement the states negotiated in May. The department also encouraged the states to conserve an additional 700,000 acre-feet over the same period and warned further cuts could follow over the next decade.

The Justice Department announced a $400 million settlement with TikTok and ByteDance resolving a lawsuit alleging violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, with $300 million payable immediately and $100 million contingent on a court vacating a prior consent decree tied to TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly. The DOJ said no determination of liability was made and TikTok did not admit wrongdoing.

In Memphis, family attorney Andre Wharton told NPR that body camera footage shows a Homeland Security Investigations agent, part of a federal deployment sent to the city at the direction of President Trump and Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, shot 25-year-old Jonah Neal without justification during a mental health crisis in late May. Wharton said the footage shows Neal's mother telling agents her son needed help and an agent audibly stating Neal held a knife, not a firearm, moments before the shooting. Neal was shot inside his home after his mother called 911 upon finding him holding her handgun and threatening suicide.

Overseas, a double-tap drone strike on a shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine killed 16 people and injured 130, with four still missing as of Friday; BBC reported the second drone targeted emergency workers already responding to the first strike, and search operations were expected to continue for up to two days.

Domestically, the Hawk Fire near Reno, Nevada burned more than 10,500 acres by Saturday evening, threatening roughly 1,000 homes and prompting Governor Joe Lombardo to declare a state of emergency for Washoe County; about 400 firefighters and three helicopters worked to contain the fire's advance overnight.

And U.S. tariffs of 50% on $20 billion of Canadian goods took effect at 12:01 a.m. ET Saturday after trade talks collapsed Friday night, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announcing matching retaliatory tariffs set for September 8.

Separately, Nancy Kassebaum Baker, the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate without following a spouse into office, died at 94. She represented Kansas across three terms from 1978 to 1997, chaired the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, and later broke with her party to endorse Democratic candidates and call for President Trump's impeachment after January 6.

On why these stories are unfolding as they are, the reporting is specific in some places and silent in others. The visa ruling rests on the judge's statutory reading, laid out in detail; the Colorado River cuts rest on the states' own May agreement plus federal drought warnings; the tariff collapse is described as negotiations falling apart before a midnight deadline without further detail on what divided the two sides. The reporting does not say whether the State Department will appeal the visa decision.
No desk boards were available this cycle to check current case, docket or filing status against the day's reporting.

The coming days carry several concrete checkpoints: whether the State Department appeals the visa ruling or attempts to reissue denials on modified legal grounds; whether trade talks resume before Canada's September 8 retaliatory tariffs take effect; whether the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation's inquiry into the Neal shooting produces a charging decision from the Shelby County District Attorney; and whether Lake Powell and Lake Mead water levels prompt deeper Colorado River cuts before the current framework's 2029 horizon. Also worth tracking: the outcome of the Hawk Fire's containment effort, further clarification on the Kryvyi Rih death toll as search operations continue, and any court action on the $100 million contingent portion of the TikTok settlement.
